facts.text: Purple crow butterflies are not one species but four similar-looking species.
From about October or November to March, large numbers of purple crow butterflies spend the winter resting in warm valleys in Maolin, Kaohsiung, in southern Taiwan.
The butterflies show a purple, shining color that can be seen only from certain angles.
In spring, mostly around the Tomb Sweeping Festival in early April, the butterflies leave the valleys and fly north across Taiwan to lay eggs.
The northward journey needs a change from the northeast monsoon to a southerly wind, dry weather, and flowering plants along the way.
Researchers mark butterflies with codes; one marked butterfly released in Maolin was found in Linnei, Yunlin, about 100 kilometers away, 33 days later.
The butterflies' route north crosses National Highway No. 3 (also called National Freeway No. 3) near Linnei Township, Yunlin County, where many were once killed by passing cars.
In 2007, the National Freeway Bureau began measures to protect the butterflies at Linnei, including a net that pushes them to fly higher and a temporary lane closure.
Along the northbound road between the 251 and 253 kilometer markers there is a net about 1,100 meters long and 4 meters high.
When 250 or more butterflies per minute cross the section, the outer northbound lane is closed; drivers only need to keep to the speed limit and do not need to slow down.
Butterfly counts at Linnei are provided by the Taiwan Purple Crow Butterfly Ecological Preservation Association.
The best time to watch the butterflies crossing is from 9 to 11 in the morning.
